directAnswer: Check the cable for printed wattage or USB PD rating, and verify with a USB-C power meter: 100W cables are marked for USB PD 3.0, while 240W cables are marked for USB PD 3.1 EPR.
summary: Identifying the wattage capability of a USB-C cable is crucial for high-wattage charging. Look for printed wattage, e-marker chips, and use a USB-C power meter for confirmation.

sections.heading: Understanding 100W vs 240W
sections.body: USB Power Delivery 3.0 supports up to 100W (20V/5A), requiring a 5A cable with an e-marker chip. USB PD 3.1 EPR supports up to 240W (48V/5A) and requires a specific EPR-marked cable, charger, and compatible device.

sections.heading: Identifying Cable Specifications
sections.body: Reputable cables often have wattage (60W, 100W, 240W) printed on them. USB-IF certified cables may display the USB logo with wattage. Thunderbolt 4/USB4 cables typically support 100W but not necessarily 240W.

steps.title: Inspect the Cable and Charger
steps.detail: Look for wattage markings like 60W, 100W, or 240W on the cable. Check the charger for PD 3.0 (20V/5A) or PD 3.1 EPR (28V/48V) specifications.

steps.title: Use a USB-C Power Meter
steps.detail: Connect a USB-C watt meter between the charger and device. Ensure the device is under load to accurately measure power draw. A 100W path shows close to 20V, while a 240W path shows 28V or 48V.

steps.title: Verify with Operating System Tools
steps.detail: On Windows, use powercfg /batteryreport to check charge rate. On macOS, go to System Settings → Battery to view charging watts. These tools provide insights but not definitive cable ratings.

steps.title: Avoid Unmarked Cables for High-Wattage Devices
steps.detail: Treat unmarked cables as 60W unless proven otherwise by a meter. For devices requiring 100W or more, use cables marked as 5A/100W or EPR/240W.

faqs.question: Can cable thickness indicate wattage?
faqs.answer: Thickness can be a hint but is not definitive. Both 100W and 240W cables have e-marker chips. Only EPR-marked cables are rated for 240W.

faqs.question: Why does my laptop charge at 60W with a 100W charger?
faqs.answer: A 3A cable limits charging to 60W. Ensure you use a 5A cable and connect to the laptop's high-power USB-C port.

faqs.question: Is a 240W cable necessary for a 100W laptop?
faqs.answer: No, a 100W (5A) cable suffices. 240W cables are for devices that negotiate higher voltages under USB PD 3.1.

caveats: A meter reading of 45W or 65W doesn't indicate cable capacity; it reflects the device's current power draw.
Do not assume a USB-C cable is safe for 5A just because it fits; unmarked cables can overheat.
